intro.en: Practical examination guide covering obstetric forceps design and classifications, specific forceps varieties, and vacuum extraction devices.

items.summary: A paired metallic instrument engineered to grasp the fetal head and exert traction along the pelvic curve to effect vaginal delivery.

blocks.title: Instrument definition and design
bullets: Two-bladed metal instrument designed to grasp, rotate, or deliver the fetal head during assisted vaginal birth.
Engineered to provide traction while minimising maternal genital lacerations and neonatal cranial compression.

groups.label: Outlet forceps
bullets: Fetal scalp is visible at the introitus without the need to part the labia.
Bony fetal skull has reached the pelvic floor and rests on the perineum.
Sagittal suture aligns in the anteroposterior diameter or within 45 degrees of rotation (ROA, LOA, ROP, LOP).

groups.label: Low forceps
bullets: Leading bony landmark of skull, excluding caput, is at station +2 or lower, but not on the pelvic floor.
Head rotation may be 45 degrees or less from the direct occipito-anterior position.
Head rotation may exceed 45 degrees, encompassing occipito-posterior positions.

groups.label: Mid-cavity forceps
bullets: Fetal head is not palpable or less than one-fifth palpable on abdominal examination.
Leading bony point of skull lies above station +2 but at or below the ischial spines (station 0 to +2).
Classified into rotation of 45 degrees or less versus rotation exceeding 45 degrees.

groups.label: High forceps
bullets: High forceps is obsolete and unsafe in contemporary obstetric practice.
Application is forbidden when more than one-fifth of the fetal head remains palpable per abdomen.
Contraindicated when the presenting part resides above the level of the ischial spines (above station 0).

groups.label: Blades
bullets: Paired curved components that cradle the fetal cranium, commonly fenestrated to reduce weight and slip.
Cephalic curve conforms to the lateral contours of the fetal head to prevent focal cranial trauma.
Pelvic curve follows the curvature of the birth canal, directing tractive force beneath the pubic arch.

groups.label: Shanks
bullets: Intermediate shafts joining blades to handles, imparting mechanical reach.
Arranged either as parallel bars in long forceps or overlapping crossed bars in compact patterns.

groups.label: Articulating lock
bullets: Joint mechanism connecting the shanks to provide stability and leverage during traction.
English lock features opposing double slots that interlock on articulation.
French lock utilises a threaded screw pivot to secure the blades.
German lock combines an interlocking slot with a screw mechanism.
Sliding lock permits longitudinal glide between blades to correct for fetal cranial asynclitism.

groups.label: Handles
bullets: Manual grip area held by the clinician to direct force and apply traction.
Equipped with lateral finger guards or resting flanges to improve mechanical purchase.

groups.label: Axis traction device
bullets: Supplemental attachment employed in mid-cavity deliveries to exert traction along the pelvic axis.
Neville Barnes or Simpson assembly connects a single pulling bar behind the lock to the handle.
Milne Murray assembly attaches twin traction rods directly to the blades with a dedicated pulling grip.

viva.q: What clinical criteria define an outlet forceps delivery?
viva.a: Scalp visible at introitus without labial separation, bony skull on pelvic floor at perineum, and sagittal suture aligned in anteroposterior diameter or within 45 degrees of rotation.

viva.q: Why is high forceps completely contraindicated in modern obstetrics?
viva.a: Applying blades above station zero or when over one-fifth head is palpable abdominally carries unacceptable risks of maternal rupture, severe haemorrhage, and fatal fetal intracranial injury.

viva.q: What are the two curves on obstetric forceps blades and what is their clinical significance?
viva.a: The cephalic curve conforms to the fetal cranium to prevent slipping, while the pelvic curve follows the birth canal curve to steer traction under the pubic arch.

viva.q: What is the function of an axis traction device on obstetric forceps?
viva.a: It applies traction in the true axis of the pelvis during mid-cavity delivery, reducing required pulling force and avoiding wasteful compression against the pubic symphysis.

items.summary: Specialised obstetric forceps models engineered for outlet extraction, rotational delivery, aftercoming head in breech, or unreduced asynclitism.

blocks.title: Overview of clinical variants
bullets: Although approximately 600 distinct patterns were historically invented, only 10 to 20 designs remain in active modern use.
Selection depends on station, moulding, need for cranial rotation, or assisted breech delivery.

groups.label: Wrigley's forceps
bullets: Short, lightweight instrument measuring 11 inches in overall length with both pelvic and cephalic curvatures.
Requires modest traction, serving as the standard instrument for outlet forceps delivery.
Commonly employed at caesarean section when manual extraction of a deeply wedged head is difficult.

groups.label: Kielland's forceps
bullets: Almost straight profile featuring a negligible pelvic curve, overlapping parallel shanks, and a sliding lock.
Lacks heavy tractive leverage, which avoids pelvic sidewall shearing during rotational manoeuvres.
Chief instrument for rotational delivery in deep transverse arrest, uniquely correcting asynclitism.

groups.label: Piper's forceps
bullets: Distinguished by a marked reverse perineal curve and long dropped shanks curved backwards.
Dropped shanks keep the lock and handles below the perineum, avoiding cranial and cervical hyperextension.
Specifically dedicated to controlled delivery of the aftercoming head in vaginal breech presentation.

groups.label: Neville Barnes forceps
bullets: Classical curved instrument with prominent cephalic and pelvic curves and an English lock.
Equipped with an axis-traction apparatus for low-cavity and mid-cavity deliveries.

groups.label: Simpson's forceps
bullets: One of the earliest forceps invented, featuring an elongated cephalic curve with separated parallel shanks.
Employed in outlet deliveries in primigravidae where substantial cranial elongation and moulding exist.

groups.label: Barton's forceps
bullets: Features a hinged anterior blade and a posterior blade meeting the shank at an obtuse angle matching pelvic planes.
Specialised for rotation and delivery of transverse arrest in a flat platypelloid pelvis.

groups.label: Elliot's forceps
bullets: Similar to Simpson forceps but possesses overlapping shanks and a more rounded cephalic curve.
Equipped with an adjustable knurled pin on the handle to regulate and restrict lateral cranial compression.
Suited for outlet extraction when cranial moulding is minimal or absent, as in multiparae.

groups.label: Tucker-McLane forceps
bullets: Features solid non-fenestrated blades, overlapping shanks, and an English lock.
Utilised for rotational delivery when little or no cranial moulding is present.
Smooth solid blades rotate smoothly without catching maternal or fetal tissues.

viva.q: Which forceps is indicated for delivering the aftercoming head in a vaginal breech birth?
viva.a: Piper's forceps. Its backward-curved perineal curve and dropped shanks keep handles below the perineum, preventing cervical hyperextension while providing controlled traction.

viva.q: Why is Kielland's forceps uniquely suited for rotational delivery?
viva.a: Its minimal pelvic curve permits axial rotation without sweeping a wide arc that tears vaginal tissue, while its sliding lock corrects cranial asynclitism.

viva.q: How does Simpson's forceps differ clinically from Elliot's forceps?
viva.a: Simpson's forceps has an elongated cephalic curve designed for moulded fetal heads, whereas Elliot's has a rounded curve and an adjustable screw pin for unmoulded heads.

viva.q: What are the dimensions and primary indications of Wrigley's forceps?
viva.a: Wrigley's forceps is 11 inches long and is used for low outlet vaginal delivery and delivering an impacted fetal head during caesarean section.

image.brief: Comparative layout on a neutral grey background displaying four major obstetric forceps variants side by side: Wrigley short outlet forceps, Kielland straight rotational forceps with sliding lock, Piper breech forceps with downward perineal curve, and Simpson forceps with elongated fenestrated blades.

items.summary: An operative vaginal delivery system using negative suction pressure through a cranial cup to facilitate fetal head descent.
unsure: Comparison section states vacuum can be used on an unengaged head, whereas earlier contraindications explicitly list unengaged head as contraindicated. Modern clinical practice strictly contraindicates vacuum extraction above station zero.

blocks.title: Device principles and pressure parameters
bullets: Assisted delivery device that extracts the fetal head by establishing negative suction against the scalp via a cup.
Negative pressure of 0.8 kg/cm2 is standardly applied, primed initially at 0.2 kg/cm2 to verify application.
Cups are constructed from stainless steel, rubber, or flexible silastic, with diameters ranging from 3 to 6 cm.

groups.label: Malmstrom metal cup
bullets: Rigid stainless steel cup linked to a traction handle by a chain within a protective silicone sheath.
Incorporates a bottom plate that distributes vacuum evenly and blocks scalp entry into the suction tube.

groups.label: Bird's rigid cup
bullets: Stainless steel cup with peripheral suction tubing and a central traction handle to enable angled pull.
Supplied in anterior and posterior models, particularly useful in transverse and posterior malpositions.

groups.label: Silastic soft cup
bullets: Soft, pliable silicone elastomer cup producing smaller, symmetrical caput succedaneum (chignon).
Significantly reduces the incidence and severity of fetal scalp abrasions.

groups.label: Kiwi OmniCup system
bullets: Single-use disposable handheld system operated entirely by a solitary clinician.
Features an integral palm pump, suction release valve, traction force gauge, and vacuum level indicator.
Flexible stem permits accurate placement over the flexion point regardless of cranial orientation.

groups.label: Maternal indications
bullets: Maternal physical exhaustion in the second stage of labour.
Prolonged second stage: 2 hours without regional analgesia or 3 hours with regional block in nulliparae.
Prolonged second stage: 1 hour without regional analgesia or 2 hours with regional block in multiparae.
Maternal disorders warranting shortened second stage: NYHA class III/IV heart disease, myasthenia gravis, hypertensive crisis, or autonomic dysreflexia in spinal cord trauma.

groups.label: Fetal indications
bullets: Presumed fetal compromise or fetal distress during the second stage of labour.
Malposition including persistent occipito-posterior or deep occipito-transverse arrest.

groups.label: Abdominal findings
bullets: Cephalic presentation confirmed; fetal head must be less than one-fifth palpable per abdomen.
Uterine contractions evaluated and monitored.

groups.label: Vaginal examination
bullets: Full cervical dilatation verified; amniotic membranes ruptured.
Exact cranial position and station determined; degree of caput and moulding assessed.
Adequate maternal pelvic capacity confirmed.

groups.label: Maternal preparation
bullets: Adequate analgesia secured via pudendal block or epidural regional anaesthesia.
Urinary bladder emptied completely by catheterisation.
Detailed counselling provided and maternal informed consent obtained.

groups.label: Personnel and theatre readiness
bullets: Senior experienced operator available; practitioner skilled in emergency caesarean section.
Round-the-clock availability of anaesthetist, paediatrician, theatre, and operative staff.
Anticipation of obstetric complications with readiness to manage postpartum haemorrhage.

groups.label: General contraindications
bullets: Incomplete cervical dilatation; unengaged head with presenting part above ischial spines.
Indeterminate fetal head position; suspected cephalopelvic disproportion.
Fetal bleeding diathesis such as haemophilia; intact amniotic membranes.
Brow presentation; lack of operator experience; patient refusal.

groups.label: Specific ventouse contraindications
bullets: Gestational age below 36 weeks due to elevated risk of neonatal subgaleal haemorrhage.
Face presentation or breech presentation.

groups.label: Application steps
bullets: Identify blades; introduce left blade first with left hand in pen-grip fashion into left pelvis along right palm.
Glide blade over fetal cranium until handle depresses and shanks rest on the perineum.
Repeat with right blade using right hand into right pelvis guided by left palm; lock articulating shanks.
Grasp with middle finger at shanks and index and ring fingers over guard; apply arm traction with contractions.
Pull downward and backward, then horizontally forward, then upward along the pelvic curve.
Disarticulate and remove blades between contractions, taking off right blade before left blade.

groups.label: Clinical checks for correct application
bullets: Sagittal suture lies precisely midway between the parallel shanks.
Gap between blade fenestration and fetal head does not exceed one finger-breadth.
Forceps blades articulate and lock without resistance.

groups.label: Kielland application in deep transverse arrest
bullets: Articulate blades externally with directional knobs pointing toward fetal occiput to identify anterior blade.
Insert anterior blade first (wandering method preferred), guiding it across face to anterior parietal eminence.
Insert posterior blade along sacral hollow, articulate lock, rotate head to occipito-anterior, and extract.

blocks.title: Ventouse application and Bird's safety rules

groups.label: Cup application and flexion point
bullets: Select largest cup that passes introitus comfortably; insert sideways pressing against posterior perineum.
Seat cup over flexion point on sagittal suture: 3 cm anterior to posterior fontanelle and 6 cm posterior to anterior fontanelle.
Flexion point application promotes vertex flexion, presenting the smallest suboccipitobregmatic diameter (9.5 cm).
Confirm complete absence of maternal vaginal or cervical mucosa within the rim of the cup.
Raise initial negative pressure to 0.2 kg/cm2, re-verify clearance, then steadily increase to 0.8 kg/cm2.
Artificial chignon forms inside cup; tract during contractions perpendicularly over handle along birth canal axis.
Release vacuum and detach cup following crowning and delivery of the fetal head.

groups.label: Bird's safety criteria
bullets: Fetal head must commence descent with the very first traction pull.
Delivery must be completed within 3 pulls.
Cup detachment must not occur more than two times.
Total duration of cup application must not exceed 20 minutes.

groups.label: Ventouse complications
bullets: Maternal: Vaginal lacerations, cervical tears, annular detachment of cervix, cup detachment, failure, and postpartum haemorrhage.
Fetal: Cephalhaematoma, scalp lacerations, chignon, retinal haemorrhage, intracranial haemorrhage, subgaleal haematoma, and neonatal jaundice.

groups.label: Forceps complications
bullets: Maternal: Vaginal and cervical tears, episiotomy extension, third or fourth-degree perineal tears, bladder injury, and uterine rupture.
Maternal remote: Stress urinary incontinence, genital prolapse, vesicovaginal fistula, and anal sphincter dysfunction.
Fetal: Facial marks, facial lacerations, facial nerve palsy, skull fracture, intracranial haemorrhage, cephalhaematoma, and ocular injury.

blocks.title: Comparative evaluation of ventouse versus forceps

groups.label: Forces and anaesthetic needs
bullets: Traction force needed for ventouse is under 10 kg, compared to 10 to 20 kg for forceps.
Compressive force applied by ventouse is 0.77 kg/cm2, compared to 1.3 kg/cm2 with forceps.
Ventouse functions under simple analgesia, preferred in cardiac or pulmonary disease; forceps requires pudendal or regional block.

groups.label: Operative differences
bullets: Ventouse is non-space-occupying and assists autorotation; forceps blades occupy pelvic space.
Ventouse causes fewer perineal tears and lower PPH rates, with less long-term prolapse or incontinence.
Forceps has higher success rates and faster setup in urgent fetal distress, but has a longer learning curve.
Forceps can deliver face presentations and preterms under 36 weeks by acting as a protective cage; ventouse is contraindicated in both.

groups.label: Critical clinical considerations
bullets: Blade fenestrations lighten forceps, reduce head compression, and anchor parietal eminences to prevent slippage.
Forceps designed for rotation possess minimal or no pelvic curve.
When set on a flat table, forceps tips curve upward and cephalic curve points inward.
Trial of forceps is a tentative attempt in theatre with setup ready to convert to immediate caesarean section.
Sequential use of vacuum and forceps substantially compounds maternal and neonatal trauma.

viva.q: Where is the cranial flexion point located for ventouse cup placement?
viva.a: It lies over the sagittal suture approximately 3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle and 6 cm posterior to the anterior fontanelle, promoting optimal vertex flexion.

viva.q: What are Bird's four safety rules for vacuum extraction?
viva.a: Descent must occur on the first pull, delivery achieved within 3 pulls, maximum two cup pop-offs, and application duration must not exceed 20 minutes.

viva.q: Why is vacuum extraction contraindicated at less than 36 weeks gestation?
viva.a: Preterm neonates have delicate subaponeurotic vessels, placing them at profound risk for fatal subgaleal haematoma and intracranial haemorrhage under suction traction.

viva.q: Compare the traction and compressive forces exerted by ventouse versus forceps.
viva.a: Ventouse requires under 10 kg traction and exerts 0.77 kg/cm2 compression, whereas forceps requires 10 to 20 kg traction and exerts 1.3 kg/cm2 compression.
